1.q: בַּ⁠שָּׁנָ֣ה הַ֠⁠תְּשִׁעִית לְ⁠צִדְקִיָּ֨הוּ מֶלֶךְ־יְהוּדָ֜ה בַּ⁠חֹ֣דֶשׁ הָ⁠עֲשִׂרִ֗י
1.note: Jeremiah is using the phrase **In the ninth year of Zedekiah king of Judah, in the tenth month** to introduce a new event in the story. Use a word, phrase, or other method in your language that is natural for introducing a new event.

The **tenth month** of the Hebrew calendar includes parts of December and January on Western calendars. You could convert the Hebrew month into an approximate time on the calendar that your culture uses. However, the Jews used a lunar calendar, so if you use a solar calendar, the date will be different every year, and the translation will not be entirely accurate. So you may just want to give the number of the month on the Hebrew calendar and say in a footnote approximately what time of year that is on your calendar.

2.q: בְּ⁠עַשְׁתֵּֽי־עֶשְׂרֵ֤ה שָׁנָה֙ לְ⁠צִדְקִיָּ֔הוּ בַּ⁠חֹ֥דֶשׁ הָ⁠רְבִיעִ֖י בְּ⁠תִשְׁעָ֣ה לַ⁠חֹ֑דֶשׁ
2.note: The **fourth** month of the Hebrew calendar includes parts of June and July on Western calendars. You could convert the Hebrew day and month into an approximate date on the calendar that your culture uses. However, the Jews used a lunar calendar, so if you use a solar calendar, the date will be different every year, and the translation will not be entirely accurate. So you may just want to give the number of the day and the name of the month on the Hebrew calendar and say in a footnote approximately what time of year that is on your calendar.

The expression **the city was broken through** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. If you need to say who did the action, Jeremiah implies that it was the army of the king of Babylon. Alternate translation: [the army of Babylon broke through the city]

3.note: Leaders at that time would sit at the city gates to discuss important matters. Here, the Babylonian officials were probably sitting at **the Middle Gate** to discuss things related to how they would militarily rule Jerusalem. Because the exact specifics are unknown it is best to leave this information implicit. If it would help your readers you could add a footnote explaining that the leaders were probably discussing something related to the governing of Jerusalem.

3.q: נֵרְגַ֣ל שַׂר־אֶ֠צֶר סַֽמְגַּר־נְב֞וּ שַׂר־סְכִ֣ים רַב־סָרִ֗יס נֵרְגַ֤ל שַׂר־אֶ֨צֶר֙ רַב־מָ֔ג
3.note: The words **Nergal Sarezer**, **Samgar Nebu**, and **Sarsekim** are the names of men who were officials of the king of Babylon. The words **Rabsaris** and **Rabmag** are the titles of high officials.

4.note: Jeremiah is using **the men of war** as a common expression of the culture to mean “the soldiers.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the fighting men]
The pronoun **he** refers to King Zedekiah. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [And Zedekiah went out the way of the Arabah]

5.note: See how you translated this name in 35:11. This also occurs in verse 8.
**Riblah** is the name of a city that was ruled by the leaders of the city of **Hamath**. Alternate translation: [to Riblah which is in the territory ruled by Hamath]

Jeremiah is using **he pronounced judgments on him** as a common expression of the culture to mean “he declared him guilty and decided how to punish him.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and he declared him guilty and sentenced him]

6.note: See how you translated “Riblah” in the previous verse.

Here, **before his eyes** represents “while he watched.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [while Zedekiah watched]

6.q: וְ⁠אֵת֙ כָּל־חֹרֵ֣י יְהוּדָ֔ה שָׁחַ֖ט מֶ֥לֶךְ בָּבֶֽל
6.note: If it would be more natural in your language, you may want to put the information about **the king of Babylon** before the information about **all the nobles of Judah**. Alternate translation: [And the king of Babylon slaughtered all the nobles of Judah]

7.q: וְ⁠אֶת־עֵינֵ֥י צִדְקִיָּ֖הוּ עִוֵּ֑ר וַ⁠יַּאַסְרֵ֨⁠הוּ֙ בַּֽ⁠נְחֻשְׁתַּ֔יִם לָ⁠בִ֥יא אֹת֖⁠וֹ בָּבֶֽלָ⁠ה
7.note: The pronoun **he** refers to the king of Babylon, while the pronoun **him** refers to Zedekiah. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [And the king of Babylon put out the eyes of Zedekiah, and he bound Zedekiah with bronze fetters to bring Zedekiah to Babylon]

7.q: וְ⁠אֶת־עֵינֵ֥י צִדְקִיָּ֖הוּ עִוֵּ֑ר וַ⁠יַּאַסְרֵ֨⁠הוּ֙ בַּֽ⁠נְחֻשְׁתַּ֔יִם לָ⁠בִ֥יא אֹת֖⁠וֹ בָּבֶֽלָ⁠ה
7.note: The implication is that the king of Babylon ordered his men to do these things. You could make this explicit, as in the UST, if that would be helpful to your readers.

8.note: In this verse, the word **house** is singular in form, but it refers to all the houses of the people of Jerusalem as a group. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use the plural form of “house.” Alternate translation: [the people’s houses]

9.note: Jeremiah is using **the ones having fallen away, who had fallen to him** as a common expression of the culture to mean “the ones who had deserted to the king of Babylon.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the ones who had abandoned their own people and surrendered to the king of Babylon]
The word **Nebuzaradan** is the name of a man. The phrase **the captain of the guards** describes his position as the commander of the bodyguard of the king of Babylon.

10.note: Jeremiah is using the adjective **poor** as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [the poor people] or [the poor ones]

Jeremiah is using **who there was not to them anything** as a common expression of the culture to mean “who owned nothing.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly as in the UST.

11.note: Here, **hand** represents “agency.” Nebuchadnezzar gave this command to **Nebuzaradan** so that he would carry it out. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [through Nebuzaradan]
The word **Nebuzaradan** is the name of a man.

12.note: Nebuchadnezzar is using **set your eyes on him** as a common expression of the culture to mean “look after him.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and watch over him]

13.q: וַ⁠יִּשְׁלַ֞ח נְבֽוּזַרְאֲדָ֣ן רַב־טַבָּחִ֗ים וּנְבֽוּשַׁזְבָּן֙ רַב־סָרִ֔יס וְ⁠נֵרְגַ֥ל שַׂר־אֶ֖צֶר רַב־מָ֑ג
13.note: The word **Nebushazban** is the name of a man. The word **Rabsaris** is the title of a high official. See how you translated “Nebuzaradan, the captain of the guards” in 39:11 and “Rabsaris” and “Nergal Sarezer the Rabmag” in 39:3.

14.note: The implication is that these officials sent men who took Jeremiah. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [and they sent men who took Jeremiah]
See how you translated the similar expression in 32:2.
The words **Gedaliah**, **Ahikam**, and **Shaphan** are the names of men. Ahikam was the father of Gedaliah, and Shaphan was the father of Ahikam.

The implication is that Gedaliah was to take Jeremiah to a specific **house**. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. This could mean: (1) the house was the home of Jeremiah. Alternate translation: [to bring him out to his own home] (2) the house was the home of Gedaliah. Alternate translation: [to bring him out to the house of Gedaliah]
The pronoun **he** refers to Jeremiah. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [And Jeremiah dwelt]
Here, the word the ULT translates as **And** could mean: (1) “And.” Alternate translation: [And so he dwelt] (2) “But.” Alternate translation: [But instead he dwelt]

15.note: See how you translated the similar expression in 8:9.

Jeremiah is providing background information about something that happened before the events he has just described. In your translation, introduce this information in a way that would be natural in your own language and culture.

The expression **he was shut up** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. If you need to say who did the action, Jeremiah implies that it was the guards of King Zedekiah. Alternate translation: [when the guards of King Zedekiah had confined him in the courtyard of the guard]
See how you translated “in the courtyard of the guard” in the previous verse.

16.q: וְ⁠אָמַרְתָּ֡ לְ⁠עֶבֶד־מֶ֨לֶךְ הַ⁠כּוּשִׁ֜י לֵ⁠אמֹ֗ר כֹּֽה־אָמַ֞ר יְהוָ֤ה צְבָאוֹת֙ אֱלֹהֵ֣י יִשְׂרָאֵ֔ל
16.note: If it would be clearer in your language, you could translate this so that there is not a quotation within a quotation. Alternate translation: [and tell Ebed Melech the Cushite that I, Yahweh of Armies, the God of Israel, say this to him]
See how you translated this name in 38:7.

Yahweh is using **Behold me bringing** as a common expression of the culture to mean “I am about to bring.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [I am about to bring]

16.q: אֶת־דְּבָרַ֜⁠י אֶל־הָ⁠עִ֥יר הַ⁠זֹּ֛את לְ⁠רָעָ֖ה וְ⁠לֹ֣א לְ⁠טוֹבָ֑ה
16.note: Here, **my words** represents the things that Yahweh said would happen to the city. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [the things that I said would happen to this city, for harm and not for good]
See how you translated the similar expression in 21:10.

Here, **to your face** represents “in your presence.” Yahweh means that Ebed Melech will see these disasters happen. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [and you will see them happen on that day]

17.note: See how you translated this expression in 1:8.

The expression **you will not be given** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. If you need to say who would do the action, it would be Yahweh. Alternate translation: [and I will not give you into the hand of the men]

Here, **hand** represents “power” or “control.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [and you will not be given into the control of those men] or [and I will not hand you over to be captured by those men]

Yahweh is using **whom you fear from their face** as a common expression of the culture to mean “whom you are afraid of.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [whom you dread]

18.note: Yahweh is repeating forms of the verb **rescue** in order to intensify his expression of the idea that it conveys. If your language can repeat words for intensification, it would be appropriate to do that here in your translation. If not, your language may have another way of expressing the intensification. Alternate translation: [For I will surely rescue you]

Here, **the sword** represents being killed by enemy soldiers in war, in which people are killed with swords. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [and in battle] or [and by enemy soldiers]
Here, **fall** represents “be killed.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [you will not be killed]
See how you translated the similar phrase in Jeremiah 21:9.
